paragraphs.heading: What algae are
paragraphs.text: Algae is a name for a huge and varied collection of living things that use photosynthesis. The land plants are left out of the group. Algae run from single cells so small you need a microscope, called microalgae, up to seaweeds built from many cells that can stretch to 50 metres. Most of them, though, are single cells with no roots, leaves or stems.

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Most algae live in water, and above all in the sea. Many drift as plankton, moved passively by the water around them, while some large seaweeds hold on to the bottom with an anchor called a holdfast. Freshwater kinds include Spirogyra, which grows in threads, and the stoneworts, which look like grass. A few unusual species manage on dry ground, in soil, on rocks or in dark caves, but they still need some moisture before they become active.

paragraphs.heading: How they make a living
paragraphs.text: Most algae feed themselves through photosynthesis, and they are the chief primary producers of life in water. Their main light-catching pigment is chlorophyll a. Their photosynthetic machinery descends from cyanobacteria and gives off oxygen by splitting water. Some are mixotrophs, which combine photosynthesis with taking in nutrients from outside. A few single-celled algae have become heterotrophs or parasites, getting all their energy from outside sources.

paragraphs.heading: Many origins, one name
paragraphs.text: Algae do not form one family on the tree of life. They are polyphyletic, which means they arose several separate times in evolution. Red, green and grey algae got their chloroplasts directly from cyanobacteria living inside them. Brown algae, diatoms and some others got theirs second-hand, from a red or green alga taken inside. The group even spans cyanobacteria, which are prokaryotes, alongside photosynthetic protists, which are eukaryotes.

paragraphs.heading: From simple to complex
paragraphs.text: Only the red and brown algae and some green ones build three-dimensional bodies made of many cells. Brown, red and green algae have each gone further still, with fully separate tissues, and some brown kelps reach 50 metres. The most complex algae are the charophytes, the line that eventually gave rise to land plants. Land plants differ in one key way: their female organs wrap the young embryo in protective layers of cells, which is why they are called embryophytes.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient and useful
paragraphs.text: Algae have a long history. Fossil threads of algae from the Vindhya basin date to 1.6 to 1.7 billion years ago. People have farmed seaweed for thousands of years, with deep roots in East Asian cooking. Today algae are also grown for cattle feed, to clean up pollution, to turn sunlight into fuels and industrial chemicals, and for medicine and science.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word alga is Latin for seaweed, and it keeps that meaning in English. Its most likely source is alliga, meaning binding or entwining. The study of algae is usually called phycology, from a Greek word for seaweed.
